It's AI That Spots Fraud Before It Happens. AI is transforming financial fraud prevention by identifying suspicious transactions in real time, helping banks stop scams before money leaves customers' accounts. Written By : Mukesh Pandey | Updated at : 03 Nov 2026 04:14 PM (IST). AI-powered fraud detection helps financial institutions identify suspicious transactions and prevent digital payment scams proactively. Source : ABPLIVE AI. Financial organizations have been utilizing transaction alerts, OTPs, and post-transaction reviews to safeguard clients from financial scams for years. But with the emergence of digital payments getting quicker and fraudsters implementing novel ways of committing fraud, just detecting fraud after the money has been sent is no longer sufficient. The new era of financial security is associated with artificial intelligence (AI), which is capable of detecting suspicious activities and acting before the funds leave the client’s account. Unlike traditional fraud detection solutions using strictly defined rules for fraud detection, AI-based technologies can analyze millions of transactions at once and identify unusual patterns of behavior, estimating the chances that fraud might take place. Show Quick Read. Key points generated by AI, verified by newsroom. Traditional fraud detection is inadequate; AI offers real-time prevention. AI analyzes vast transaction data to detect unusual patterns. This allows stopping fraud and reducing false payment declines. Ongoing model testing balances security with customer convenience. As all transactions and their details are analyzed (including how often the transaction takes place, where it goes, from which device and where the user is located, as well as the client’s previous spending behaviors), suspicious transactions could be detected within seconds. How Does AI Detect A Suspicious Transaction?. Suppose a user who normally makes small payments online suddenly decides to make a large transfer to an unknown recipient. While traditional solutions might react to the size of the transaction, AI systems have the advantage of being able to analyze several contextual indicators at once and determine if the payment is legitimate. Thus, the systems can notify clients about further verification, stop the transaction, or send it for further investigation depending on the risk level and the banks’ policies. The Importance Of Real-Time Intelligence. The success of fraud prevention via AI relies on its ability to process information and adapt to new threats. The machine learning models can accumulate knowledge about suspicious behaviours all the time due to new cases of transactions and fraud. This can result in fewer fraud cases for banks, fintech companies and payment providers as well as more effective investigations and targeted interventions. Consumers will experience fewer unnecessary payment refusals because intelligent systems will be able to identify rightful suspicious behaviours and avoid unnecessary declines. However, these systems should be regarded as not being perfect. The use of low-quality data, sophisticated fraud methods and incorrect models can produce false alarms or skip suspicious transactions. title: Agentic AI Being Considered in Banking
excerpt: . SHARE. Artificial Intelligence Agents are being adopted by Kenya’s Central Bank (CBK) to help in processing payments, fraud detection, credit risk assessment and customer service. Robert Mudida the CBK Director of Research said on Monday, that despite adoption of AI agents, the bank would maintain human oversight over decisions made using the technology. “Agentic AI is at the highest level because these agents are being trained to take over critical decisions that are being done by human beings,” said Mudida. “It has great opportunities but also great dangers, so we are going slowly, but there are opportunities of using agents in areas like payments,” Mudida said. Kenya’s financial regulator is also exploring more than 300 artificial intelligence applications to improve operational efficiency, including testing a new AI-powered chatbot. “We are trying to move as fast as possible, but we are very aware of AI governance, which is very important to ensure the security of data,” Mudida noted. CBK’s Research Department is already using AI for microforecasting in volatile economic conditions and nowcasting to fill data gaps and provide the Monetary Policy Committee with near-real-time information on the state of the economy. The regulator’s exploration of AI agents comes as financial institutions increasingly use artificial intelligence to support payment processing, fraud detection, credit risk assessment and customer service. title: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute starts operations with AI focus; names interim CEO
excerpt: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute starts operations with AI focus; names interim CEO. The interim CEO of the new body is Alan Lim, head of MAS’ financial infrastructure and AI office. Summarise. Tan Nai Lun. Published Tue, Nov 3, 2026 · 06:35 PM. 阅读简体中文版 (beta). MAS says FFI will unite financial institutions in the sharing of practical ideas in implementing AI, develop good practices for deploying agentic AI, and beef up risk management in the use of AI. PHOTO: BT FILE. [SINGAPORE] The Future of Finance Institute (FFI) began operations on Tuesday (Nov 3) with a focus on AI in finance, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said. It will bring financial institutions together to share practical experience in implementing AI, develop good practices for deploying agentic AI, and strengthen the management of risks from the use of AI, said MAS. Its managing director Chia Der Jiun said: “(The FFI) will seek to anchor key capabilities in Singapore, and connect the ecosystem to accelerate innovation and support safe adoption of new technologies. ”. This comes as banks and regulators become increasingly concerned about the risks that rapid AI adoption may bring to the financial industry. Alan Lim, head of the financial infrastructure and AI office at MAS, will serve concurrently as the interim CEO of FFI. He will lead FFI’s strategy and operations as it builds out its programmes and deepens partnerships in the financial and technology ecosystems, MAS said. THE BUSINESS TIMES INSIGHTS. title: Hong Kong Becomes First Banking Regulator to Require Identity Credentials for AI Agents
excerpt: By Kyle Belmonte Published: Nov 03 2026, 1:55 AM EST. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp. Hong Kong's central bank debuted its banking AI governance project for autonomous AI agents on Monday, making history as the world's first banking-specific governance initiative targeting a structural gap that existing financial regulation cannot fill: autonomous AI systems that can move money, negotiate contracts, and instruct other AI systems without a human authorizing each step have no standard way to prove who deployed them, what they are permitted to do, or who is liable when they act. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) unveiled Project SAGE — Securing Agentic Finance with Governance and Enablement — at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026, backed by a 22-member cross-sector expert group and a formal discussion paper asking what "Know Your Agent" (KYA) standards should require in practice — a question economists warn carries systemic financial stability stakes , not merely operational risk. What Makes AI Agents Different From Generative AI?. Traditional generative AI tools operate on a prompt-response model: a user asks, the AI answers, and a human decides what to do with the output. Agentic AI is architecturally different. Given a goal and a set of tools — database access, payment APIs, messaging systems — an AI agent plans a sequence of actions, executes them, observes the outcome, and replans, all without human confirmation at each step. In banking, the distinction has concrete and high-stakes implications. A generative AI tool might help a loan officer draft a credit memo. An agentic AI system could independently identify lending opportunities, pull credit files, calculate risk-adjusted terms, route for approval, execute the disbursement, and log the transaction — entirely without a hand on a keyboard at any intermediate step. Add multi-agent orchestration — where one AI agent instructs a chain of sub-agents — and a single human instruction can trigger a cascade of autonomous banking actions across multiple regulated entities, currencies, and time zones. The HKMA explicitly cited use cases the industry is already building: AI agent-driven consumer payments and shopping, enterprise treasury and procurement management, and machine-to-machine pay-per-use billing for digital services. Each scenario raises a version of the same unsolved question: who, exactly, is responsible for what the agent did?. Project SAGE's Four Pillars: From Use-Case Validation to Kill Switches. Project SAGE is structured around four areas of work that together constitute a full governance stack for agentic finance, as laid out in the HKMA's governance discussion paper :. Use-case validation ensures that proposed applications are tested in controlled settings — grounded in evidence from the HKMA's own GenAI Sandbox++ program — before live deployment at scale. Agent identity and authorization is the most novel pillar, and the one the HKMA has framed under the shorthand "Know Your Agent. " This track will design what identity credentials for AI agents should contain, how they should be issued, and how counterparties should verify them. Interoperable standards addresses the cross-border dimension: agentic payments crossing from Hong Kong to the Chinese mainland to a digital asset settlement layer need shared technical protocols if liability is to be traced when something goes wrong. Governance, legal liability, and consumer protection examines the hardest structural question: how to allocate responsibility when an AI agent authorized by a bank causes a loss — especially when that agent was itself instructed by another AI agent. title: LGMS banks on AI-powered cybersecurity solutions for top-line growth
excerpt: PETALING JAYA: Main Market-listed cybersecurity firm LGMS Bhd ’s expanding portfolio of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered solutions could unlock new revenue opportunities, although meaningful earnings contributions will depend on their commercial adoption and monetisation. In a report, Mercury Securities Sdn Bhd said management highlighted the growing sophistication of cyberattacks, with malicious actors leveraging AI to automate attacks, identify vulnerabilities and gain unauthorised access to systems. LGMS’ presentation showed that 65% of investigated cyber intrusions originated from exposed online vulnerabilities, followed by stolen passwords at 30% and infected computers at 5%. Meanwhile, only 18% of cyber incidents were detected by organisations’ own security tools, while 47% were identified through external parties and 29% through the damage caused. “With AI enabling cyberattacks to be executed at greater speed and scale, we believe the evolving threat landscape could support longer-term demand for LGMS’ cybersecurity solutions, particularly as businesses accelerate digitalisation and AI adoption,” Mercury Securities said. Against this backdrop, the research firm said LGMS’ adoption of AI could also improve operational efficiency by automating repetitive and time-consuming tasks. For instance, its large language models (LLM)-assisted Static Application Security Testing or NOVA solution uses LLMs to identify vulnerabilities in application source code, potentially reducing the manual effort required for security assessments. StarPicks. A SMALL VILLAGE, A WIDER WORLD. Similarly, AI-assisted threat analysis could help cybersecurity specialists identify and prioritise potential threats more efficiently. “We believe greater automation could enhance employee productivity and support the scalability of LGMS’ cybersecurity services, potentially improving operating margins over the longer term,” it said. However, LGMS’ near-term profitability could remain under pressure from elevated operating expenses associated with continued AI-related investments. Mercury Securities said meaningful earnings contributions from its new solutions would depend on the pace of commercial adoption and the group’s ability to monetise them. While pending greater visibility on their revenue contributions, the research firm maintained its earnings forecasts, with financial year 2026 (FY26) and FY27 revenue growth assumptions of 4% and 11%, respectively, and operating expenditure margins of 66% and 67. 6%. It also kept its FY26 and FY27 earnings estimates unchanged at RM9. 3mil and RM9. 7mil, respectively. The research firm maintained its “hold” recommendation and 49-sen target price, based on an unchanged 23 times target price-to-earnings multiple, benchmarked against the three-year historical average of domestic peers with comparable operations and applied to its FY27 estimated earnings per share of 2. 1 sen. Separately, LGMS has introduced five homegrown cybersecurity solutions designed to strengthen protection across different stages of cyberattacks. Mercury Securities said the offerings could broaden the group’s service portfolio, create cross-selling opportunities and support its transition towards recurring revenue. title: Regional banks want purpose-built AI
excerpt: Business. General. Regional banks want purpose-built AI. Data privacy and regulatory compliance are top barriers to adoption, Fico survey finds. PUBLISHED : 4 Nov 2026 at 01:00. NEWSPAPER SECTION: Business. Listen. Share. Facebook. Reddit. Copy Link. Senior banking leaders across Asia-Pacific have made it clear that general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) is insufficient for financial services, as three-quarters believe AI tools used in banking must be built specifically for financial services, not adapted from consumer applications. A survey conducted by the global data analytics and credit-scoring company Fico found 77% of banking leaders say it is "extremely important" that AI tools used in banking be built specifically for financial services. Only 23% viewed such specialisation as merely "somewhat important". "Financial institutions operate under regulatory scrutiny that most consumer technology companies don't face," said Dattu Kompella, managing director in Asia-Pacific for Fico. "Banks need AI models that are explainable, auditable and designed from the ground up for compliance. Off-the-shelf consumer AI doesn't meet that bar. ". Banking leaders identified regulatory and governance concerns as the primary barriers to AI adoption, not technology or cost. Data privacy and security emerged as the top concern, cited by 42% of respondents. A further 21% identified regulatory and compliance risk as their biggest worry, while 21% flagged model transparency and explainability as critical. Only 16% cited computing cost or infrastructure as a barrier. "The barriers aren't about capability or price," said Mr Kompella. "Banks are concerned about trust, auditability and the ability to explain decisions to regulators. That's exactly why purpose-built AI for financial services matters. It's designed with those constraints in mind from day one. ". FRAUD PREVENTION. Banking leaders see immediate high-impact applications for generative AI. More than 60% identified fraud and scam detection as the area where generative AI could most improve operations in the next 12 months. A further 21% cited underwriting decisions, 15% customer-facing digital banking services, and just 3% regulatory compliance monitoring. This focus reflects both the urgency of the scam epidemic across the region and the potential for AI-powered behavioural analytics to detect patterns human analysts might miss, noted Fico. Banking leaders expect purpose-built AI to become standard quickly. Nearly half (46%) expect task-specific AI models to be deployed in fraud, compliance and underwriting operations within 1-2 years, while 26% expect adoption within 3-5 years. Only 26% report having already deployed such models. Across the region's leading banks, the priorities are clear. Beyond fraud prevention, 64% identified credit underwriting and lending decisions as the back-office process that would benefit most from purpose-built AI. A further 18% cited regulatory compliance monitoring, 10% customer due diligence, and 8% internal policy and business operations review. The focus for purpose-built AI is moving from whether to adopt to how to execute a plan, said Mr Kompella. Banks will need to invest in domain-specific models designed for financial services, supported by cleaner data infrastructure, faster integration with legacy systems, and clearer governance frameworks, he noted. The poll was conducted in August during the Fico Banking Leaders Forum in Bali, with the respondents 51 senior executives and corporate banking leaders from Asia-Pacific institutions. KEYWORDS. Huntington Banchshares aims to galvanize its small-business banking franchise by equipping entrepreneurs with agentic AI tools. Processing Content. It provides small-business owners with a suite of agents Huntington says can streamline noncore operations, recapturing time that can be spent on fundamentals. "If you're part of the studio, you would constantly have access to tools you can use to manage your business from day to day," Huntington President Brant Standridge told American Banker. Huntington's move aligns with a broader trend involving lenders and tech companies providing small business operators with access to AI tools. Huntington's solution combines a number of functions into what it characterizes as a front-to-back small- business operating system. It encompasses financial tasks such as banking and payments, as well as nonfinancial tasks including human resources, marketing and inventory management. The 1866 Studio also has a module for aspiring entrepreneurs that helps them navigate the steps involved in starting a business, Konduru said. Standridge likened the 1866 Studio's design to a phone with apps loaded onto it. title: Banks navigate AI risks solo as regulators play catch-up
excerpt: AI Agents. Banks navigate AI risks solo as regulators play catch-up. By Maria Volkova. About Maria. twitter. mvol4ok. Published November 03, 2026, 8:53 a. m. EST. |. Updated November 03, 2026, 11:26 a. m. EST. 5 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: AI agents are creating a new gray area for banks around fraud and liability, leaving financial institutions to their own devices in determining best how to protect customers and themselves in the absence of clear rules. Expert quote: "Statutory changes are hard and take a long time, and nobody wants to wait. The banks don't want to wait because they like the idea of there being more payments and less friction in payments. Customers don't want to wait because they love AI doing this for them. Merchants don't want to wait because they like selling things. " — Julie Hill, Dean, University of Wyoming College of Law. WASHINGTON — The rapid emergence of AI agents and their growing adoption among consumers have created a new set of risks for banks to contend with — and they're largely on their own to mitigate those risks. Without established rules of the road for AI agents, banks are left to navigate the technology's promises and pitfalls in real time while preserving the safety and soundness of their systems. Industry insiders expect that prudential regulators will eventually address these questions around AI agents. Until then, banks will have to develop their own protocols to mitigate risks and safeguard their systems. "The agents are here now, and rulemaking takes a while," said David Zaring, a professor of legal studies and business ethics at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School of Business. "In the medium-future, or in the short-term future, I think banks may be walking the tightrope without much of a net. ". AI agents are bots that have been empowered by a consumer to make financial decisions on their behalf — actions ranging from tracking down hard-to-find concert tickets to completing online purchases. While the potential benefits for consumers and commerce are potentially significant, the technology also introduces a range of risks for banks. Those risks present themselves in two distinct flavors: fraud on the one hand and faster deposit outflows on the other. While industry stakeholders see both as concerns, many view fraud as the more immediate threat as banks grapple with determining whether transactions initiated by AI agents are legitimate. Central bank: Significant share of Dutch workers are in jobs that AI could transform. Tuesday, 3 November 2026 - 07:00. A significant share of Dutch workers hold jobs in which the rise of artificial intelligence could bring a major change, the Netherlands’ central bank said in a new report on AI’s economic impact. A key finding is that the effects on the labor market and the broader economy remain uncertain and will depend in part on how companies actually deploy the technology. According to De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), one-quarter of Dutch workers are in occupations in which AI could accelerate the performance of at least half of their tasks. At a threshold of 40 percent of tasks, the share rises to half of all workers. The differences across occupations are large: software developers, linguists, and accountants face a substantial potential impact, while cleaners face relatively little. Researchers emphasized that their measure indicates where AI can support or automate tasks, not what will happen to employment. That outcome remains uncertain. AI could take over tasks, help workers accomplish more, and enable new products and services. As a result, DNB said greater use of AI needs to lead to fewer jobs. AI could also either amplify or dampen price increases. Its effect on inflation will depend on how quickly investment rises and whether companies can produce more and more cheaply with the technology. For many people, the content of their work is likely to change. DNB said employers would be wise to include provisions in collective labor agreements for the reskilling and upskilling that will be needed. The report also concludes that AI could make the Netherlands more productive and prosperous. The country starts from a favorable position, the researchers said, but more work remains. Smaller firms in particular have ground to make up, even though AI could be especially valuable for them by giving them access to knowledge and capabilities that would otherwise be out of reach. The Netherlands does not need to develop the most advanced AI models itself to benefit, DNB said. Companies do need to develop the most advanced AI models and the necessary computing power, as well as the ability to switch providers easily. The central bank also said the government should carefully weigh any additional national requirements for AI and ensure that successful companies have sufficient room to invest and grow. Reporting by ANP.

Rex Africa has launched an AI-powered banking platform in Nigeria, combining everyday financial services with an artificial intelligence assistant designed to help customers make decisions about their money. The platform, launched on October 30, features Rex Atlas, an AI-powered financial agent that analyses customers’ financial history and provides guidance on saving, investing, borrowing and managing financial risks. Unlike conventional banking apps that primarily help customers check balances and complete transactions, the finance company says Atlas is designed to help users understand their financial habits and make decisions based on their individual circumstances. The launch comes as Nigeria makes progress in expanding access to financial services but continues to struggle with financial well-being. According to the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation and Advancement (EFInA), formal financial inclusion increased from 64% in 2023 to 73% in 2026. However, only about one in four Nigerian adults is financially healthy, suggesting that access to financial services has not necessarily translated into financial security. The company is positioning its AI assistant as a way to address part of that gap. We built Rex with AI at the heart of the banking experience, not as an additional feature,” Opeyemi Emmanuel, the company’s chief technology officer, said. The company says its proprietary infrastructure, RexCore, was built with artificial intelligence integrated from the beginning. Atlas sits on top of this infrastructure, providing the conversational interface through which customers can receive financial guidance. Similar read: Grey secures CBN IMTO approval to formalise inbound remittance rails in Nigeria. What Rex Africa offers. Beyond the AI assistant, the platform provides savings, credit, and payment services for individuals and businesses. Its individual offerings include RexSave for flexible savings, RexVault for fixed-term savings, RexFlex for credit and RexCard for payments. Businesses can use RexPOS to accept payments and RexCredit to access financing. The firm operates through Rex Microfinance Bank Limited, which the company says is licensed and regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Eligible deposits are covered by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation, subject to applicable limits. The finance company also says it has a lending business and a Banking-as-a-Service portal that supports accounts, collections and payouts. It also describes itself as Nigeria’s first AI-native bank, arguing that artificial intelligence is embedded in its banking infrastructure rather than added as a separate feature. However, the company has not provided independent evidence establishing that it is the first Nigerian financial institution to adopt this model. It has also not disclosed specific figures for customer numbers or transaction activity, saying only that it has attracted thousands of individuals and hundreds of businesses since launch. The bigger test will be whether its AI assistant can offer useful, reliable financial guidance beyond the basic functions already available through digital banking apps. How it handles customers’ financial data and the accuracy of its recommendations will also matter as the platform grows. title: Sterling Bank, Aké Festival seek cultural integration, Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: Sterling Bank, Aké Festival seek cultural integration, Artificial Intelligence. 03 November 2026 10:39 am WAT. By The Sun. Follow Us on Google. By Henry Akubuiro. One of Nigeria’s leading banks, Sterling Bank, has renewed its partnership with the Aké Arts and Book Festival, one of Africa’s foremost gatherings of writers, artists and thinkers, as the festival returns to Lagos from 19 to 21 November 2026 with a conversation on Africa’s place in an increasingly technology-driven world. Now in its 14th edition, the festival will explore the theme ‘Native Intelligence’, which examines the relationship between the knowledge Africans have developed and passed down for generations and the artificial intelligence systems increasingly influencing how people live, learn, work and communicate. The theme stems from a simple fact: Africa was thinking long before machines were. The elder, the proverb and the folktale represent systems of knowledge refined over centuries. Today, artificial intelligence is changing how stories are told, how elections are fought and how truth is reported across the globe. Yet questions remain about how adequately African languages, experiences and cultural contexts are represented in the technologies increasingly shaping the world. For Sterling Bank, which has supported the festival since 2018, the partnership represents a continued investment in the people and ideas shaping Africa’s cultural and intellectual future. Over the years, Aké has provided a meeting point for established and emerging writers, artists and thinkers, bringing together more than 1,000 creative voices and creating opportunities for African stories and perspectives to reach wider audiences. Commenting on this year’s convening, Donatus Okpako, Chief Marketing Officer at Sterling Bank, told Daily Sun, “Every society has an intelligence, the instinct and judgement employed to read a situation and solve a problem. Africans have always had it in abundance. As AI reshapes how we work, bank, vote and learn, the real concern is whether Africa’s own ways of thinking help shape the technology it relies on. For fourteen years, Aké has placed African ideas at the centre of global conversations. That is a platform worth standing behind. ”. ‘Native Intelligence’ does not treat African knowledge as a relic to be kept behind glass – it treats it as a living intelligence with a claim on the future. Over three days, novelists, poets, journalists, technologists, filmmakers and scholars will examine who gets to decide what counts as knowledge. They will also ask the question at the heart of the festival: whose intelligence are we building the future on?. Lola Shoneyin, Founder and Director of the Aké Arts and Book Festival, said at the festival preview in Lagos, “A machine knows only what it has been fed, and it has not fed much of us. Native Intelligence is about power: who decides what is true, what is worth remembering, and whose voice the future speaks in? Sterling understands our goal to support and celebrate creativity on the African continent and beyond. We are delighted to work with them again. ”. The festival programme includes book chats, panel discussions, film screenings, conversations and poetry performances and music. Registration is open at akefestival. org. Sterling Bank Limited is a member of Sterling Financial Holdings Group. With a heritage of more than 60 years, the bank has evolved from Nigeria’s pre-eminent investment banking institution to a trusted provider of retail, commercial, and corporate banking services. It has been committed to transforming lives through innovative solutions, exceptional service, unwavering integrity, and a steadfast focus on its HEART strategy, which centers on Health, Education, Agriculture, Renewable Energy, and Transportation.
